text: The last lesson treated a GPU as indivisible — you get a whole one, or you wait. That's true by default, but there are two real ways around it for workloads that don't need a full GPU: MIG and time-slicing.

MIG, available on A100, H100, and similar data-center GPUs, splits one physical GPU into up to seven fully isolated instances at the hardware level. A workload on one instance cannot be slowed down or crashed by a workload on another instance of the same card — the isolation is real, not a scheduling courtesy.

Time-slicing instead lets multiple workloads share one GPU by rapidly switching between them in time. A device plugin config can advertise four schedulable GPU slots on one physical card, but unlike MIG, there's no memory isolation — one workload can still exhaust shared memory or slow down everyone else on that card.

MIG trades flexibility for real isolation and only works on newer hardware. Time-slicing works on any GPU but offers no isolation at all. Which one you reach for depends entirely on whether the workloads sharing a card can be trusted not to step on each other.
Both exist for the same underlying reason. Next up, lesson thirty-one: the real cost of GPU idle time — why sharing mechanisms like these matter in the first place.
